title: GST on Sales Returns: How to Adjust Tax, Stock and Customer Refunds
summary: Learn how GST on sales returns works: issuing a credit note, adjusting output tax, updating stock and refunding customers, with examples and time limits.
body_markdown:
# **GST on Sales Returns: How to Adjust Tax, Stock and Customer Refunds**


A return by a customer after the sale does not mean that the process ends there. The **GST on sales returns** concerns three factors all together: your GST that you've declared, the inventory in your storage, and the amount due to the customer. Failing to balance one factor against the other two results in inconsistent accounts, which eventually shows itself in GST Notice or stock audit failure.


To handle a **sales return under GST** in the right manner means to generate a correct credit note, declare it on time, update your stock accordingly, and deal with the refund in connection with the previous invoice. This guide gives detailed information on how to do it with examples provided.


## **Effect of sales return on GST**


You will have accounted for output tax by issuing the initial invoice on which GST was levied. In case of the customer returning the goods, the supply of the goods is deemed to be cancelled, and so does the output tax.


Under GST, the sales return cannot be accounted for through subtraction from your subsequent return as stipulated by the law in Section 34 of CGST Act. The **GST credit note** is issued in case of sales return, and it gives you the ability to reduce the amount of output tax.


### **Purpose of a credit note**


The ****[credit note](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/what-is-credit-note) is issued by the supplier against the previous tax invoice. According to Section 34 of CGST Act, it can be issued for the following reasons:


As per rule 53, credit note must contain:


- Words 'credit note' and a serial number
- Date of issue
- Name, address and GSTIN of supplier
- Name, address and GSTIN (if applicable) of the person to whom the credit note is issued
- Number and date of original invoice
- Return of value of goods, taxable value and tax rate
- Reversal of CGST, SGST or IGST
- Place of supply (if applicable)
- Signature/digital signature


Reference to the original invoice is very important. The credit note without reference to the original invoice will cause a mismatch of data on the portal.


In case you have an e-invoicing requirement, then the credit notes too have to be reported on the Invoice Registration Portal, along with the invoices.


## **Time period to reduce GST**


You cannot reduce the tax liability at any time as per the provision which has been split into two parts.


- Details in the credit note shall be furnished in the[GST return](http://etswipe.in/blog/article/gst-refund-key-definitions-interest-rates) of the month in which credit note has been issued.
- This is required to be done **no later than 30th November** in the subsequent year after the year in which the original supply was made or date of furnishing of annual return, whichever is earlier.


The time period is calculated from the date of original supply and not date of return. For example, let us consider a sale in March 2026 in FY 2025-26. Then the deadline for furnishing the credit note will be 30th November 2026 or GSTR-9 filing date whichever is earlier. Now as we have reached the last week of October 2026, the remaining time available to file returns for FY 2025-26 is just a few weeks.


For a sale in August 2026 in FY 2026-27, the deadline is 30th November 2027.


## **Conditions to decrease output tax liability**


From 1st October 2025, Section 34(2) has another condition. You will decrease your tax liability only if the following applies:


- **When the customer is registered:** then the input tax credit corresponding to the credit note, if they have claimed any, has been revoked by them.
- **When the customer is unregistered:** then the tax has not been charged to anyone else on this transaction. Usually in sales returns, this condition will be fulfilled as the customer receives their payment, along with GST.


Check the updated language on the CBIC website because GST laws are always subject to change, and even the Finance Act 2026 has modified certain conditions regarding post-sales deductions.


In practice, inform your registered customers about the issuance of the credit note as they need to revoke the credit in their GSTR-3B. Otherwise, there will be a mismatch between your tax liability and theirs.


## **Where credit note should appear in your returns**


The credit note will be disclosed in[GSTR-1](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/what-is-gstr-1-conquering-common-errors-with-faqs) under credit/debit notes in Table 9B. Both registered and unregistered recipients have been classified separately. Then the deduction gets reflected in[GSTR-3B](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/understanding-gst-return-exploring-the-basics-of-gstr-3b) during the same period, resulting in a reduction in output tax payable either in cash or credit.


When the credit note is issued any month later than the invoice is filed in that month, it's perfectly fine. You should declare it in the month it was issued, provided the deadline above hasn't expired yet.


## **Refund of credit note to the customer vs. adjustment of tax**


Both the above are quite similar, but there is a difference between them.


‍


**GST refund from the customer** refers to you paying back the money. This could be done via bank transfer, UPI, or through setting off against his pending dues. It's a business deal between you and your buyer.


‍


**GST adjustment of returned goods** is a legal procedure in which you adjust your output tax by reporting the credit note in your return. In this case, it's not the government paying back the customer.


## **Practical handling of returns**


This is an intelligent process flow you can use.


**1. Receive and verify:** Document what has come in terms of quantity and quality. Damage and shortage must be recorded since this is what will determine where these products will land in either of the three: available stock, damaged goods, or waste.


**2. Relate the return to its corresponding invoice:** Make sure that the invoice number is indicated on the return document. Many accounting issues start here because there is no return without an invoice.


**3. Update the stock:** Increase the available stock of accepted items using their original cost. Damaged or rejected items must be updated separately along with any write-offs.


**4. Create the credit note:** Prepare the note for the amount of accepted goods.


**5. Make an agreement with the customer** either by refunding the total amount including GST or holding it in the credit against any future purchase made by the customer in the future and ensuring that the customer’s ledger reflects the same.


**6. Prepare the GST returns:** Include the credit note in GSTR-1 and allow the adjustment to reflect in GSTR-3B.


If it is a return of goods, ensure that the movement of the goods back to you is properly documented through delivery challan and E-way bill wherever required.


### **Example 1: Return of all the quantity**


If you have sold 40 units at ₹2,500 each to a registered customer of your own state then you have a taxable value of ₹1,00,000, a GST of 18% being ₹18,000 and an invoice value of ₹1,18,000.


The customer returned 40 units on account of wrong specifications. You inspected those units, added them to the inventory, and issued a credit note of ₹1,00,000 along with ₹9,000 CGST and ₹9,000 SGST.


### **Example 2: Partial Return**


Same invoice, but only 10 units are returned by the customer. The credit note will be ₹29,500 for ₹25,000 being the price of 10 units at ₹2,500 each plus GST of ₹4,500. This will mean that the other 30 units will be treated as an actual sale. The credit note will relate to the same invoice.


## **When the credit note will not reduce your tax**


There could be situations when there is a sale which has been returned beyond the specified time limit. You could still accept the return and refund the amount to the customer. You may also issue a commercial credit note in such a case. However, it won’t fall under[Section 34 of the CGST Act](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/gst-on-credit-notes-under-section-34-of-the-cgst-act-conditions) . Hence, you cannot reduce your output tax liability. Similarly, there could be instances where the conditions of Section 34(2) are not satisfied and hence a reduction of tax cannot be made.


## **Conclusion**


A sale return affects your tax returns, your inventory accounts and your customer’s accounts, and all three must agree. With everything reconciling to the original invoice, accounting becomes easy. But missing the deadline in Section 34 means that you may be forced to write off tax you didn’t even retain. Create a return checklist and ensure all returns are in order prior to 30th November annually.


## **FAQs**


### **1. Am I allowed to lower the GST without giving a credit note?**


No. GST credit note in Section 34 is the right way to deduct the output tax from a sales return.


### **2. For how long is the validity period of the GST credit note for sales return?**


The information must be submitted by 30th November within the following financial year after making the supply or filing an annual return, whichever occurs first.


### **3. Do I have to pay back GST along with the cost of sale?**


Usually yes, in case when you want to reduce your tax with the help of a credit note. Otherwise, the client will get back the total amount including the GST he has paid for the product.


### **4. What happens if the client is an unregistered person?**


You are still able to issue the credit note in such a case, provided that the tax liability arising from the supply hasn't been transferred elsewhere.
